paragraphs: Scope and boundaries: This page covers only O*NET-SOC 49-3051.00, Motorboat Mechanics and Service Technicians, who repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment on boats with inboard or inboard-outboard engines. It excludes outdoor power equipment mechanics primarily working on small air-cooled engines, bus and truck mechanics primarily working on commercial vehicles and diesel systems, and ship engineers managing engine-room system operations. Disassembly and assembly, electrical work, fuel handling, and sea trials must follow repair shop authorization and local laws.

How to assess fit: Using an entirely fictional fault work order and test data, see whether you can describe the diagnostic sequence, disassembly and inspection records, replacement plan, torque and calibration requirements, and sea-trial verification steps, and identify three safety confirmation points. Keep this a paper simulation without operating real equipment or accessing fuel systems.

Who may fit: People willing to troubleshoot step by step and confirm with tool measurements, accept outdoor work and contaminated environments, notice abnormal mechanical sounds and data deviations, and complete energy isolation and safety checks before disassembly. Note: If you tend to replace parts based on experience without testing, dislike recording the process, or bypass lockout/tagout, compare adjacent directions first.

Note: All exercises below are editorially designed paper simulations. They involve no real equipment or fuel systems and do not authorize equipment operation, electrical work, lockout/tagout, or sea trials. Decisions involving repair work, electricity, and water safety must follow manufacturer materials, repair shop procedures, and local rules.

The official definition of Motorboat Mechanics and Service Technicians (O*NET-SOC 49-3051.00) is to repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment on boats with inboard or inboard-outboard engines. The scope excludes outdoor power equipment mechanics primarily working on small air-cooled engines, bus and truck mechanics primarily working on commercial vehicles and diesel systems, and ship engineers managing engine-room system operations.

entries: Operational monitoring and initial fault assessment: Start engines and listen for abnormalities such as smoking, excessive vibration, or misfiring, and read instruments to assess operating conditions.
Disassembly, inspection, and fault location: Use hand tools and measuring instruments to disassemble and inspect engines, locating faulty parts and hidden damage.
Parts replacement and assembly: Replace parts such as gears, magneto points, piston rings, or spark plugs, and reassemble to specifications.
Routine servicing: Replace consumables such as engine oil and filters on schedule, and inspect belts, pumps, and connections.

Calibration and system repair: Adjust carburetor mixtures, electrical points, and timing in water-filled test tanks; adjust generators and replace damaged wiring; and service cooling, propulsion, and steering systems.

Sea-trial verification and customer explanations: Install engines in boats and test them at different speeds on waterways, read temperature gauges to assess cooling, explain repair procedures to customers, and record inspection and test results.
Records and handover: Record symptoms, test data, replacement parts, calibration parameters, and sea-trial results, and complete repair work orders and fee explanations.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET survey): 86% of respondents have face-to-face discussions daily; 80% work outdoors exposed to all weather conditions daily; 63% work in open vehicles or operating equipment daily; 71% encounter contaminants such as exhaust, dust, or odors daily; 66% make decisions affecting others or organizational resources daily; and 65% use their hands to operate tools and parts continually or almost continually.

Key capabilities: Troubleshoot through testing steps; proficiently disassemble and assemble mechanical and electrical components; apply specified torque and calibration; assess cooling and propulsion systems; complete sea-trial verification when conditions permit; and follow safety procedures such as energy isolation and lockout/tagout. Basic knowledge of marine engines, electrical systems, and hydraulics is needed.

Preparation and training: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 3, typically requiring vocational school training, related work experience, or an associate degree, plus 1—2 years of on-the-job training. The O*NET national training directory lists marine maintenance and ship repair programs at multiple institutions, from certificates to bachelor's degrees. Listed national certifications are STCW-related mariner certificates of competency from the US Coast Guard's National Maritime Center.

Professional judgment: Key decisions concern accurate fault location, assembly and torque compliance with repair documentation, normal operation after calibration, and acceptable sea-trial conditions. Stop work and report to the repair supervisor when uncertain or beyond your authority. Do not conduct trials with unresolved safety hazards.

Main outputs: Restored engine and propulsion system operation; reviewable test data and repair records; lists of replaced parts and calibration parameters; sea-trial verification results; and customer-confirmed repair work orders and fee explanations.

Conclusion: Motorboat mechanics and service technicians' core output is restoring reliable operation of marine engines and propulsion systems. Outdoor power equipment mechanics focus on small air-cooled engines; bus and truck mechanics work on commercial vehicles and diesel systems; farm equipment mechanics work on agricultural machinery; mobile heavy equipment mechanics work on heavy construction equipment; and ship engineers manage engine-room system operation and seaworthiness. Adjacent occupations are presented for comparison only and do not imply automatic transfers or mutual recognition of qualifications.
The comparison draws on the official O*NET 49-3051.00 description and tasks and the O*NET profiles of adjacent occupations. It is an editorial synthesis, not a job recommendation.
Comparison dimensions: This page compares core work and outputs, key differences from this occupation, and which preferences each option may better suit, to help clarify your direction.

Difference from Outdoor Power Equipment and Other Small Engine Mechanics: This occupation handles cooling, propulsion, and electrical systems of inboard and inboard-outboard engines and requires on-water trials. The adjacent field primarily handles small air-cooled gasoline engine equipment such as lawnmowers and generators.

If you prefer repairing commercial vehicles and diesel systems, compare bus and truck mechanics and diesel engine specialists; if you prefer agricultural machinery, compare farm equipment mechanics and service technicians; if you prefer heavy construction equipment, compare mobile heavy equipment mechanics; if you prefer responsibility for engine-room operations, compare ship engineers.
People entering through marine repair education programs or on-the-job mentoring
First learn tool use, repair documentation, and safety procedures, including energy isolation and lockout/tagout. Perform simple disassembly and assembly and maintain records under supervision.
Repair personnel primarily handling diagnosis and parts replacement
Maintain traceable test data, replacement part records, and calibration parameters. Review repeat repairs and abnormalities through repair shop procedures.
Staff responsible for system repairs and sea-trial verification
Follow repair documentation for torque and assembly sequence, check trial waters and weather, and test by increasing speed in stages.
Career changers
First build knowledge of marine engines and propulsion systems, reading repair documentation, and safety procedures. Use entirely fictional work orders and test data for paper simulations.

Exposure varies across diagnosis and repair, sea-trial verification, and routine servicing.

No occupation-specific accident/health/repeat-repair rates were obtained. OSHA supports mechanisms involving hazardous energy during maintenance, not accident probabilities for this occupation.

ai_impact_table.responsibility_intro: The steps below describe the sequence of human controls when motorboat mechanics and service technicians use tools: input verification, conditions of use, output review, and recordkeeping.

responsibility_steps.说明: Check work orders, engine models, and fault descriptions, and confirm the availability of parts catalogs, repair documentation, and safe conditions.

Before disassembly and repair, control and verify hazardous energy under applicable procedures. Controlled startup testing/sea trials are a separate step: restore operation through authorized procedures while maintaining personnel protection, ventilation, and waterway safety. Do not force a startup while locked out.
Have a person confirm disassembly inspection results, assembly torque, and calibration parameters, and review operating conditions during sea trials.
Record symptoms, test data, replacement parts, calibration parameters, and sea-trial results.
Stop and report to the responsible manager when hidden damage, work beyond authorization, or safety hazards arise.

components.definition_block: The official definition of Motorboat Mechanics and Service Technicians (O*NET-SOC 49-3051.00) is to repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment on boats with inboard or inboard-outboard engines. The scope excludes outdoor power equipment mechanics primarily working on small air-cooled engines, bus and truck mechanics primarily working on commercial vehicles and diesel systems, and ship engineers managing engine-room system operations.

fermat_decision_card.summary: Use an entirely fictional fault work order and test data for a paper simulation, checking the diagnostic sequence, disassembly inspection records, replacement plan, and sea-trial verification steps. A paper simulation does not authorize equipment operation, lockout/tagout, or sea trials.
fermat_decision_card.title: Motorboat Mechanics and Service Technicians

hero.quick_answer: Motorboat mechanics and service technicians (O*NET 49-3051.00) repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment on boats with inboard or inboard-outboard engines: start engines and listen for abnormalities such as smoking, excessive vibration, or misfiring; replace oil and filters on schedule; disassemble and inspect engines to locate faulty components, replace parts such as gears and piston rings, and reassemble; adjust carburetor mixtures, ignition points, and timing in water-filled test tanks; inspect and repair or adjust propellers and drive shafts; adjust generators and replace damaged wiring; install engines in boats and test them at different speeds on waterways, reading temperature gauges to assess cooling; recondition parts using machine tools; and explain repair procedures to customers. Record inspection and test results throughout.

description.text: Motorboat mechanics and service technicians (O*NET 49-3051.00) repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment on boats with inboard and inboard-outboard engines. This page explains official tasks and work context, the US BLS 2025 median annual wage of US$57,550 and 6% growth for 2024—2034, mainland Chinese proxy wages for resident services, repairs, and other services, AI task boundaries, fit signals, and entry routes.

subject.name: Motorboat Mechanics and Service Technicians
subject.summary: Motorboat mechanics and service technicians (O*NET-SOC 49-3051.00) repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment on boats with inboard or inboard-outboard engines: start engines and listen for abnormal sounds and vibration; replace oil and filters on schedule; disassemble, inspect, and replace components such as gears and piston rings; adjust carburetors and ignition timing; inspect and repair propellers and drive shafts; repair generators and wiring; install engines in boats and test operation on waterways; and record inspection and test results.
